newsitem.title: USA: China seen top US cotton mkt for fifth straight yr.
newsitem.headline: China seen top US cotton mkt for fifth straight yr.

text.p: China should remain the top U.S. cotton market for a fifth consecutive year in 1997-98 (August-July), despite holding stocks that account for about 42 percent of the world total, U.S. analysts said Thursday.

"It is conceivable if they decided to make a policy change, they could rely on their stocks to supply their internal needs," Carol Skelly, fibers analyst for the U.S. World Agricultural Outlook Board, told Reuters
But USDA has seen no evidence yet that Chinese officials are planning any such action, she said.
China has been the world's top cotton importer for the past three years and the top U.S. cotton market for the past four.

In the meantime, its cotton stocks have risen from 6.1 million 480-pound bales--or 23 percent of the world total--in 1993-94, to an estimated 15.7 million bales in the 1996-97 marketing year that just ended.
As those numbers indicate, "they don't really have a shortage of domestic cotton," Skelly said.
But what China does have is a policy that encourages imports by supporting domesend, chief statistician for the International Cotton Advisory Committee (ICAC).
Even with the rising stocks, it's cheaper for textile mills to import cotton, he said.
"They recognize they do have large stocks and that their policy is expensive," Townsend said. But any change is likely to come gradually, he said.

Cotton producers in China's far western cotton regions don't have many other crops they could grow. Ratcheting the domestic cotton price below the world level "would be socially disruptive," Townsend said.

But China has other options for curbing imports, if it decides to take that action. State-run textile mills have long been banned from importing cotton. A similiar restriction could be imposed on foreign-partner joint-venture mills.
Or China could subsidize textile mills purchases of domestic cotton to make it competitive with foreign cotton.
Skelly agreed any change was unlikely to come soon. But China is far more likely to try to reduce imports than to dump its cotton stocks on the world market.
"They would prefer to export value-added goods," rather than the raw cotton, she said.
According to USDA estimates, China imported 3.4 million bales of cotton in 1996-97, about half of which came from the United States.
USDA forecasts China's total imports in 1997-98 to drop to about 2.7 million bales, but it still should remain the top U.S. market, Skelly said.
ICAC forecasts China's cotton imports to drop to 2.5 million bales in 1997-98 and 2.0 million in 1998-99, he said.
"I think the U.S. will maintain its (50-55 percent) of a falling market," Townsend said.

China's four-year reign as the top U.S. cotton market is not without precedent. In the 1980s, Japan was the number one market for five consecutive years. Since then, high labor, land and other costs have cut its textile industry in half.
In time, other countries may also move ahead of China on the U.S. top ten cotton market list.
Brazil now rivals China as the world's number one cotton importer and Mexico is a growing market for U.S. cotton, Townsend said.
